work.title: Engagements that show how the work is done.
work.lead: Some projects are public by their nature, a national blockchain product, or a platform you can click. Others are described by sector, without names or identifying detail. That is the ordinary price of working inside organisations that do not publish their architectures, and I would rather pay it than work around it with hints.

insights.title: I give the thinking away and charge for the doing.

method.title: Architecture on demand.
method.lead: This practice's method is older than this website and simpler than it sounds: architectural effort is a cost, so I spend it only where it reduces a risk the organisation cannot afford to carry. The rest of the effort goes into building the working system. Its continuous variant, architecture as a service, means architectural oversight bought when a decision worth overseeing appears, instead of a staff position that has to justify itself.

doctrine.title: Proportional to risk
doctrine.body: The measure of how much architecture is needed is the cost of reversing the decision, not the size of the project. System boundaries, the data model, identity, integrations, these are expensive to reverse, and they get analysis, a record and a review. At the bank that meant a full architecture board over a core system replacement; on a product build, one decision log and a one-page sketch of boundaries. Both were the right amount, because both were proportional.

doctrine.title: The last responsible moment
doctrine.body: I defer a decision until further delay would start removing options, because the most expensive architectures are built from answers to questions nobody has asked yet. In practice: foundations that cannot be added cheaply later go in from the first migration; features wait for proof of need; and every deferred decision has a written retreat path, down to fallback versions of dependencies.

doctrine.title: Executable architecture
doctrine.body: A standard no machine checks is an opinion with good meeting attendance. The architecture model lives in the repository, validation returns an exit code and works as a pipeline gate, and deviations exist only as dispensations with expiry dates. This is what evolutionary architecture calls fitness functions, except mine actually stops the build.

doctrine.title: The minimal artifact: a decision
doctrine.body: If one thing is to survive out of all architecture documentation, let it be the decision log: context, options considered, why the others were rejected. I also keep build-vs-buy tables with a verdict on every rejected option. Diagrams go stale; the reasons for decisions do not.

method.lineageBody: I did not invent these rules, I assembled them from things others tested and named. Proportionality to risk is the thesis of George Fairbanks's Just Enough Software Architecture. Executable architecture is the fitness functions of Neal Ford and Rebecca Parsons's Building Evolutionary Architectures. The decision log in this form was described by Michael Nygard. The last responsible moment comes from Mary and Tom Poppendieck's lean software development, and the figure of the architect who writes code rather than judging it from above, from Martin Fowler's essay on architectus oryzus. My contribution is elsewhere: in the discipline of applying these rules in environments that usually consider them too light, a bank, a regulated fintech, a plant floor.
method.processLead: No two engagements are identical, but the order is usually the same.

process.title: Conversation
process.body: No deck and no commitment. What interests me is what specifically hurts and what happens if nothing changes. If that conversation shows I am not the right address, I say so immediately.

process.title: Reconnaissance
process.body: A few days spent seeing the actual state of things: the architecture, the process or the code, depending on the problem. I talk to the people who maintain the system, not only to those who commissioned it.

process.title: Diagnosis and direction
process.body: A report that works in the boardroom and in the engineering team: what is a risk, what can be left alone, what should be done in what order and roughly what it costs. Always with options rather than a single recommendation.

process.title: Delivery or oversight
process.body: Either I build, or I steer decisions alongside the client's team. In both cases documentation and decision records are written with the work, not after it.

process.title: Handover
process.body: Runbooks, an environment reproducible from the repository, and a walkthrough with the team taking over. I consider an engagement successful when it can be ended without harming the client.

method.aiBody: I use AI agents in day-to-day software delivery, one reason a small practice can keep more than a dozen production repositories moving at once. Exactly the same rule applies as with clients: the model proposes, tests and deterministic validation rule, a person answers for the result. Specifications and decision records are the source of truth; the code is their consequence.

engage.title: How an engagement usually starts.
engage.lead: There are no packages or price lists on this site, because a sensible scope can only be set after a conversation about the problem. The shapes of engagement follow directly from the method: architecture on demand is effort sized to a single decision, architecture as a service is the same discipline sustained over time. Both are described below, alongside diagnostics and delivery.

forms.title: Diagnostic
forms.body: A short, intensive look at the architecture, the AI plan or security. It ends with a report and a prioritised roadmap. The most common starting point, partly because it is easy to close if going further makes no sense.

forms.title: Architecture on demand
forms.body: Architectural effort applied to one decision, at the moment it appears: system boundaries before a major project, the data model before the first migration, a platform choice before a vendor contract is signed. Options analysed with a verdict against each rejected one, the decision recorded, a retreat path written down. No retainer and no quarterly commitment; the organisation comes back when the next decision worth overseeing appears.

forms.title: Architecture as a service
forms.body: The continuous variant of the same method, for organisations without a staff architect: standards with a lifecycle, review of changes with architectural consequences, decision and dispensation registers, quality gates in the pipeline, presence at the decisions that are expensive to reverse. Billed in days per month; the oversight does not have to justify its existence by producing artifacts, because it is not a salaried post. This is the shape the practice started as.

forms.title: Ongoing advisory
forms.body: A standing presence at the intersection of the board and technology, broader than architecture alone: reviewing decisions, pressure-testing vendors, technology strategy. For organisations that do not need a full-time CTO or are currently looking for one.

forms.title: Delivery
forms.body: Building a system end to end and handing it to the client's team or a maintenance partner. With documentation, decision records and runbooks written alongside the code.

engage.selectivityBody: A few. This practice scales through method and tooling instead of hiring. That means sometimes you wait for a slot, and sometimes I say I cannot take a project in a given quarter. I consider that more honest than putting forward a team I do not know.
engage.pricingBody: Agreed in conversation, once the scope is understood. Publishing ranges without context either underprices a badly defined problem or filters out conversations that were worth having.

about.title: A practice, not an agency.
about.lead: ArchXS exists around one method: architecture on demand. Architectural effort is sized to the risk of a specific decision, and in its continuous variant, architecture as a service, it replaces a staff architect where a staff position would not hold its own. The method's precondition is a combination that usually drifts apart with seniority: architecture at scale and uninterrupted hands-on delivery.
paragraphs: The practice grew out of two decades in organisations where an architectural mistake is expensive: eight years in global card payments under PCI-DSS, enterprise architecture at a state development bank and on a core banking replacement, technology leadership at a regulated fintech, a national-scale blockchain product, and most recently technology in manufacturing, from the plant floor to e-commerce.

Code is written in parallel. More than a dozen active production repositories, backend systems in two independent ecosystems, web and mobile applications, industrial integrations, custom identity-server extensions, open-source tooling. That body of work is how recommendations get tested before they are handed to someone else.

That is where the scope of this site comes from. You will not find a biography or conference photographs, because they are not the subject of the work. You will find positions, evidence and writing from which a way of thinking can be judged, and that is the only thing anyone really buys in advisory work.

resources.title: Things to take.
resources.lead: No sign-up, no email address, no paid continuation. If a resource is worth anything, it should be useful to someone who never gets in touch.
resources.ossLead: Repositories are published under the practice's GitHub account. Some were built for specific projects, others because there was nothing suitable to use.

oss.name: Enterprise architecture toolchain
oss.desc: A define → document → govern → maintain cycle with the model in git. A purpose-built DSL, a compiler to ArchiMate 3.2 Open Exchange validated against the Open Group XSD, an architecture description in the shape of ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, standards with a lifecycle, dispensations with expiry dates, and a validator that returns an exit code in the pipeline.

oss.name: Identity server extensions
oss.desc: SPI for Keycloak 26: an authenticator and credential provider for sign-in by cryptographic signature (EIP-191) with replay protection, OTP as a second factor, passkeys, custom screen templates and deployment documentation.

oss.name: @archxs/keycloak-wagmi
oss.desc: An MIT-licensed npm package: a wagmi connector for IdP-managed EVM wallets, implementing EIP-1193 and supporting smart accounts (ERC-4337).

oss.name: Accounting assistant for sole traders
oss.desc: A self-hosted alternative to accounting SaaS: Polish e-invoicing under the FA(3) schema, JPK filings, social-security and income-tax returns, a deadline calendar, expense-document OCR and a chat-driven agent. MIT licence, around 180 tests.

oss.name: Language-model evaluation arena
oss.desc: A public tool for comparing models on multi-turn tasks: one Elo ladder for models and humans, server-side validation of every ranked game, per-move cost and latency telemetry, a hallucination ranking. The user's API key never leaves the browser.

resources.writingLead: Most of the practical material is in the essays, checklists and question sets are part of them, not a separate download.

sections.heading: Data controller
sections.body: The controller of personal data submitted through this site is Dariusz Tyszka, running an advisory practice under the ArchXS name. Contact for data protection matters: contact@archxs.com.

sections.heading: What I collect
sections.body: Only what you provide yourself: name, email address, optionally an organisation name, and the content of your message. The site does not use cookies for marketing or profiling. Visit statistics, where collected, are aggregated and do not identify individuals.

sections.heading: Purpose and legal basis
sections.body: Form data is processed to answer your enquiry and potentially to begin working together, on the basis of the controller's legitimate interest in communicating with people interested in the services (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR), and once an engagement begins, to perform it (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR).

sections.heading: Recipients
sections.body: The contact form and call booking are operated by external service providers who process the data solely on my behalf. Email is handled by a mail hosting provider. I do not sell or share data for marketing purposes.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: Correspondence that does not lead to an engagement is deleted no later than twelve months after the last contact. Data relating to a completed engagement is kept for the period required by tax law and limitation periods for claims.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: You have the right to access your data, rectify it, erase it, restrict processing, port it, and object to processing based on legitimate interest. You may also lodge a complaint with the Polish data protection authority (Prezes Urzędu Ochrony Danych Osobowych).

It is not legal, tax or investment advice and cannot replace analysis of a specific case. Applying the approaches described here in your own environment is at your own risk.
